You installed Claude Code inside Cursor? For 11 hours on Oct 29, the version in Cursor's marketplace tried to plant an SSH backdoor. Up to 5,000 people got it.

One line in Terminal tells you if you're one of them.

What happened:
→ A modified build of the Claude Code extension, version 2.1.313, went up on Cursor's marketplace from 2:27am to 1:35pm PT
→ It wasn't built by Anthropic. Cursor says the official distribution isn't affected
→ It collected your hostname, username, Git email and public IP, then tried to add an attacker's SSH key and open a reverse tunnel
→ Cursor took the marketplace down, the attacker's server is offline, and the fix is version 2.1.314

Check on a Mac:
grep -qs svc-telemetry ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && echo "key found" || echo "No key found; machine not impacted"

If it says "key found": don't just uninstall. Cursor says the backdoor leaves scripts that keep running. Use their cleanup script, then rotate every password and token that machine could reach.

My take: an extension with "Anthropic" in the name runs with your permissions, not Anthropic's. Coding agents can touch your terminal, your keys and your repos. Check the publisher and the version before you hit update, the same way you'd check a link before you click it.

Did you update Claude Code in Cursor on Thursday?

We're still in the early innings of AI transformation. Varick estimates the market for AI transformation will grow 100x over the next 3 years.

Finance is one of the best places to start, for a few reasons:

- Most of the time is spent waiting. One invoice exception takes 25 minutes of work, but 11 days to clear.
- Finance leaves a better data trail than any other function. Every invoice, approval, and journal entry is timestamped somewhere, even if half of it lives in Excel.
- Much of the work is rule-based. You can't afford for agents to hallucinate in the finance function, and by incorporating heavy determinism, you de-risk the agents.

In the article below, our COO Eyad breaks down the exact playbook we've used to roll out AI in finance at some of the largest companies in the world.

If you're working on agents in finance, or you're an FDE, this playbook is a gold mine.

a16z's Connor Love and Erin Price-Wright on what startups should take from SpaceX and Tesla, and when building it all yourself actually makes sense:

Connor: "We can look to Elon for a lot of answers here. I mean, it's not a crazy statement to say really the few modern-day companies that have built anything at scale are probably SpaceX and Tesla. And if you look at how Elon and his team have built those businesses, it's been, one, very vertically integrated."

"I take the ideology that you shouldn't vertically integrate everything. I mean, again, if you're building a super exquisite system like a missile that is doing something very unique, you kind of have to because you have to control the exquisiteness. You have to control the cost."

Erin: "SpaceX and Tesla were doing first of their kind. There didn't exist an industrial base in the US to support them, and so they had to build it themselves. I think where there are high-quality suppliers, you should use suppliers."

Connor: "In a lot of ways they had to make those choices because they didn't have any other opportunity. But in the end, it's actually just that mantra of design for manufacturing that now exists within all these systems companies."

a16z's Connor Love says building for defense is how America builds for everything else, because once you can make the parts "to quality and to cost," new markets start to make sense:

"When you build many systems, you also require many subsystems below that. There are really interesting military systems being built today. The corollary: by building towards defense, you also build for a different industry."

"The subsystems that go into some of our military systems are the exact same subsystems that are going to go into the future robotic systems. It's the actuators, the motors, the valves and switches."

"When you can build those to quality and to cost, then all of a sudden other markets that maybe weren't viable make sense... You're going to have this robotic wave that will come in America."

"AI can't turn a wrench yet. They will eventually. And that will be enabled by all that, actuators and switches and subsystems that we built... And we're not going to have to rely on factories in China."

"As you build an industrial base, an industrial base can be used for many things. Down to the component level, I just think we don’t have enough of it in America."

a16z's Erin Price-Wright says factory technicians can now retool production lines with AI in 20 minutes, a job that used to take an outside integrator 3 months:

"Historically, if you're setting up a line with a lot of automation, you really need to be producing a lot of one single thing. That's how you get the cost down, and how you justify investing in a pretty bespoke manufacturing line."

"But what we're seeing across our portfolio is that manufacturing technicians themselves have the intuition, and now the software tools, to change the economics of producing low-volume, high-mix on the line."

"A manufacturing technician, not necessarily someone with a college degree or who's studied software engineering, can now use these tools to reprogram and reconfigure their lines on the fly, because they understand the manufacturing process."

"Instead of calling a systems integrator, which takes 3 months and hundreds of thousands of dollars to reconfigure a line, you can have a manufacturing engineer use Claude and do that in 20 minutes. That's been a real game changer."

text:
Brian Schimpf of @AndurilTech on why industrial production is a deterrent in itself, and why technological superiority alone won't win a war:

"These wars are protracted, they are industrial in scale, and if you were to bring it down to one variable, the amount of kilograms that you can throw at each other turns out to probably be the single most important factor."

"I think the technical superiority is a huge advantage. We're not gonna just outproduce China on like dumb ammunition, right? Like that clearly we have to have an edge around our space capabilities, how we can sense, how we can confuse them, how sophisticated our weapons are."

"But I think the part that got so clear outta Ukraine was that industrial production has a deterrence factor... it is critical for winning a conflict."

"When most of the war games with China show that we'd be out of munitions in... like eight days, that's not a deterrence factor really anymore."

"I think the belief for a long time was that [technological superiority] was sufficient, but a low number of really exquisite weapons is not gonna win a conflict."

@SchimpfBrian (September 2025)

text:
Chris Power of @HadrianInc says in wartime simulations, the US runs out of munitions in about a week, and it takes 2-3 years to restock:

"Out of every war game we run, we run out of munitions and missiles, whatever, in like six to seven days. And then it takes about two to three years to refill that battery of, 'Hey, you now have more missiles to shoot.'"

"Every single war basically, if it goes hot, both sides throw everything they've got at each other over a time period. And it's basically then if it gets protracted, how fast can you reconstitute?"

"We shoot all our missiles in one week and then we have none for two years. That is how kind of terrible the situation is."

"The only thing we can do is focus on, honestly, attritable systems, because if you kill a carrier and they've got that range, there's nothing we can do about it."

"A lot of attritable mass... We basically blow everything in the seven days. We got to have the manufacturing battery to be able to refill the clip extremely fast."

@2112Power (September 2025)

When prediction market volumes exploded during the Nov 2024 election, I remember being as worried as everyone else that they'd fall off a cliff.

But markets are one of the most powerful technologies in the world, and Tarek and Luana have understood since the beginning that consequential events happen every day.

Fast forward to today, Kalshi’s $40b announcement won’t do much for brand awareness. Everyone knows the name. Fewer people know how much the business has expanded into non-sports, institutional, and perps.

No celebration at Kalshi HQ today, but congrats on the milestone @mansourtarek_ @luanalopeslara @Kalshi. Proud to be your partners on this journey.

quoted_tweet.author: Tarek Mansour
quoted_tweet.text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.
